newsitem.title: FRANCE: Arafat bars French adviser from PLO pension fund.
newsitem.headline: Arafat bars French adviser from PLO pension fund.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat has barred a French economic adviser, Gabriel Banon, from handling a Palestinian pension fund, according to documents obtained by Reuters.

In a December 21 letter, Arafat told the New York bank which holds part of the pension fund that Banon and his consultancy firm no longer represented the Palestinian Authority and instructed the bank to stop dealing with him.

"Mr Gabriel Banon and/or Strategic and Development Policies Advisor (SDPA) do no longer represent the Palestinian National Authority in its dealing with your firm," Arafat wrote to Morgan Stanley Asset Management, confirming a November 4 letter from Palestinian Justice Minister Freih Abu Meddein.

Arafat's office confirmed the authenticity of the letter which named an Israeli-Swiss businessman, Arie Gilon, chairman of Zurich-based Belesta Asset Management, as Banon's successor. Gilon confirmed to Reuters that he had been appointed on November 24.

Senior Palestinian officials said Arafat had picked Jewish businessmen with Israeli ties because he believed they would have a better chance of persuading Israel to hand over the money deducted from Palestinian employees of the administration during the Israeli occupation of the West Bank and Gaza since 1967.
Last July, Arafat paid $250,000 out of the fund to an account controlled by the Moroccon-born businessman at Banque Monod in Paris.
Banon, who still describes himself as the PLO leader's officially appointed economic adviser, told Reuters the money was transferred to cover his expenses.
He said he had originally sought $450,000 but had told Arafat last month he would waive the remaining $200,000 in the light of the problems it had caused for him.
"If you divide $250,000 by the 36 months I worked on the pension fund, it comes to less than $7,000 a month. That doesn't even pay my office rent," Banon said.

He said he had advised Arafat to transfer the entire pension fund to the Paris bank to avoid U.S. taxation, since at that time the United States would not grant the Palestinian Authority an exemption it gives to sovereign states.
Abu Meddein, who is chairman of the pension fund, travelled to Paris in September and halted that transfer.
After weeks of argument, he convinced the PLO leader to remove Banon from dealing with the fund.
"We decided to put him aside because his ideas did not coincide with our ideas," Abu Meddein told Reuters in Gaza. "The $250,000 he received were his fees."

Another businessman with ties to Arafat, Pierre Rizk, former intelligence chief of the Christian Lebanese Forces militia, has since sued Banon in a Paris court for a cut of the proceeds from the pension fund.

In an interview with Reuters, Banon said: "My mission on the pension fund is drawing to an end. Other missions are continuing." He displayed a file of letters of mission signed by Arafat in 1994 and 1995.
The Palestinian leader first took on Banon, a French citizen with U.S. residence, in December 1993, shortly after the PLO signed a peace agreement with Israel negotiated in Oslo.
Arafat did not respond to repeated requests from Reuters for comment on Banon's role, although his office confirmed he had signed the letter barring Banon from the pension fund.

PLO officials said Arafat's original aim had been to attract foreign investment through an intermediary he believed enjoyed the confidence both of the Israelis and the international business community.

But from the outset the choice was controversial among Palestinian officials. Arafat attended the inauguration of Banon's Paris SDPA office in 1994 against the advice of the general-delegate of Palestine in France, Leila Shahid.

Banon sat in on talks with donors at the World Bank office in Paris and Western officials were surprised to see him sitting behind Arafat at an international aid conference staged by the French government last January.

Western diplomats said Arafat's management style and the presence of extraneous advisers at aid talks, were among factors that made some donor nations reluctant to disburse promised aid to the Palestinians.
Under an accord signed in November 1994, the Israelis agreed to hand over to the Palestinian Authority 430,456,563 shekels in accumulated pension contributions worth about $155 million.

A first payment of $80 million was transferred from the Euro-Trade Bank in Tel Aviv to Morgan Stanley last year after lengthy wrangling over whether the money should be paid in shekels or dollars. The second instalment is still outstanding.
Banon said it was due soon and his work would then be done.
"I was a symbol because of my religion. The president never wanted to blacken me in any scandal," he said.
